notes.story: [Let the headline sit for a few seconds.] “What do you think they were hiring for?” [Take a guess from the room.] The U.S. Nautical Almanac Office had two vacancies for people to do calculations. The civil service exam included trigonometry and astronomy. Their calculations helped produce tables that sailors used to navigate by the sky.
notes.transition: Let’s look at what a room full of computers looked like.
notes.materials: New York Times, May 2, 1892, p. 8. Scan reproduced by Dan Nguyen: https://danwin.com/2013/02/the-first-mention-of-computer-in-the-new-york-times/ · Page attribution: https://srtate.github.io/old/100.f17/lectures/UNCG-CSC100-F17-LECT3-ComputerScience.pdf

notes.story: At the NACA Lewis laboratory, human computers plotted data from photographs of wind-tunnel instrument readings. One test could produce scores of data points, and working through them could take days.
notes.transition: Now look at how that work changed when machines could do more of the arithmetic.

title: From the computer room to your desk

notes.point: From the computer room to your desk
notes.story: These are milestones in who could afford calculation at scale. Government laboratories and other large institutions could staff computing rooms. Large businesses used machines like the IBM 1401 for recurring payroll and billing. Desktop spreadsheets put what-if questions, like whether to hire, within reach of much smaller businesses.
notes.transition: Say you run a small design studio and you’re turning down client work. Could you afford to bring someone on?
notes.materials: NASA: https://www.flickr.com/photos/44494372@N05/53912325323 · IBM: https://www.ibm.com/history/1401 · System photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BRL61-IBM_1401.jpg · VisiCalc: https://www.computerhistory.org/timeline/1979/ · Later screenshot: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Visicalc.png · UNIVAC: https://www.census.gov/about/history/bureau-history/census-innovations/technology/univac-i.html

title: Two billable days or three?

notes.story: A small design studio is turning down client work. The owner wants to know how many billable days would cover a hire costing €5,000 per month. Assume four weeks and €500 per billable day. At two days a week, they’re €1,000 short. Ask “What if they can bill three days a week?” [Advance.] Revenue rises to €6,000 and they’re €1,000 above cost. Ask “What if it takes a few months to get that busy?” [Pause.] The spreadsheet lets the owner explore what would have to be true for the hire to pay for itself.
notes.transition: Look at the questions the studio can now try.

cue: Can a small studio cover the cost of a hire?

notes.story: Start with the question in the overlap. The owner can check whether the hire covers its cost. [Advance.] Watch the circle grow around the other two questions. What if work starts slowly? What if we hire part-time? With a spreadsheet, running another scenario is easy enough to try.
notes.transition: The cost of trying a new question fell. What happens when the cost of trying a new tool falls?

title: What becomes worth building?

notes.story: A reusable quote template is already practical. [Advance.] What if the studio could turn a client brief into a draft quote and checklist? AI can make the first version cheaper to build. The tool itself can work with or without AI. See whether it saves time for someone who writes quotes.
notes.transition: Players of The Gibson App had been asking for another way to play.

cue: AI can make a first version cheaper. Try a tool for one job, with or without AI.

title: The Gibson App

notes.story: Players had long asked to play on a computer. The Gibson App already had gameplay on iOS and Android. Another platform adds work to build, test and support. [Advance.] Here is a browser gameplay preview of Add Index Finger. AI-assisted development helped the existing team pursue browser gameplay.
notes.transition: Here, the additional thing worth trying was a way to play on a computer.

title: Guitar gameplay on a computer

notes.story: Supporting iOS and Android is already part of the work. [Advance.] The existing team can now pursue another way for people to play, by bringing gameplay to the browser. That opens a way to reach people who want to play on a computer.

cue: Another way for players to get started

title: GymNative · From paper to phone

notes.story: I wanted to put the paper aside, log my workouts on my phone, and see whether I was getting stronger. I saw other people at the gym logging on paper too. [Advance.] Haguegym can give its members an app with its equipment and workouts already set up. Members can scan a code and get straight to logging.
notes.transition: A general tracker could already do part of this. What would make a logger for one gym worth trying?
notes.materials: Local Haguegym captures with fictional workouts.

cue: I wanted to put down the paper, log on my phone, and see my progress.

title: A logger set up for this gym

notes.point: A logger set up for this gym
notes.story: Using a general tracker is already practical. [Advance.] AI-assisted development made a first version tailored to one gym practical to try. The Haguegym pilot is underway. The question is “Will members come back and log their next workout?” The work is deciding what the gym should configure, how a member opens it and logs a first set, and what we would need to see to keep going. I’d look for members returning to log another workout, and ask where anyone got stuck.
notes.transition: Now let’s look at a tool for one room in a coworking space.
notes.materials: Haguegym pilot underway. Use the repeat-workout question without claiming an outcome.

cue: Pilot underway. Will members log another workout?

title: Is the meeting room free at two?

notes.point: Is the meeting room free at two?
notes.story: [Let people recognize the sheet.] “The current system works beautifully, provided you’re already standing in front of it.” [Pause.] What would it take to answer the same question from your desk?
notes.transition: Think about it from the coworking operator’s side.

title: What’s practical for a neighbourhood co-working space?

notes.point: What’s practical for a neighbourhood co-working space?
notes.story: A sheet on the door is cheap, familiar, and does the job when you’re there. [Advance.] For one shared room, a small online booking tool is now reasonable to try. Someone can see what’s free and reserve it from their desk.
notes.materials: Use the same circle expansion as in the earlier examples.

cue: Maybe a more sophisticated system is possible.

title: Book online. Subscribe to the room calendar.

notes.point: Book online. Subscribe to the room calendar.
notes.story: I built the first version in about an hour. Members can check availability and book from their desks. They can also subscribe and see room availability alongside their own calendars.
notes.transition: Think about your own work. What’s practical to try now?

title: What’s practical to try now?
body:
A spreadsheet only you know how to run
A task you do by hand every week
A service you repeat for every client

notes.story: Cheaper calculation let businesses ask more questions about what they offered. Cheaper software lets businesses and entrepreneurs try small tools that can improve what they offer their clients. [Advance to expand the Practical circle. Pause.] What part of your work could you make easier? I enjoy helping people understand what’s possible, choose a small experiment, and see whether it helps. If something came to mind, I’d love to hear about it over a drink.
